source.root_cause: main() never validates that argc >= 3 before dereferencing argv[1] and argv[2]. The argv array elements at indices 1 and 2 are accessed via double indirection (mov rax,[argv+off]; mov rax,[rax]) without any bounds check on argc. When invoked with fewer than 2 arguments, argv[1] or argv[2] is NULL, and the second-level dereference (mov rax,[rax] where rax=0) causes a NULL pointer dereference, resulting in SIGSEGV.
source.description: Two crash paths exist: (1) 0 arguments -> argv[1] is NULL -> crash at 0x1193 (mov rax,[rax] with rax=0); (2) 1 argument -> argv[2] is NULL -> crash at 0x117b (mov rax,[rax] with rax=0). Both are NULL pointer dereferences at address 0x0, producing SIGSEGV and process termination (DOS).

argv[1]/argv[2] is NULL when argc < 3
double indirection: mov rax,[argv+off] loads NULL pointer into rax
mov rax,[rax] dereferences address 0x0 (NULL pointer dereference)
SIGSEGV -> process crash -> denial of service

preconditions.description: The binary must be invoked with fewer than 3 arguments (argc < 3). With 0 arguments, argv[1] is NULL (crash at 0x1193). With 1 argument, argv[2] is NULL (crash at 0x117b).

preconditions.necessity: The NULL dereference only occurs if the attacker controls how the binary is invoked. If the binary is always called with exactly 2+ arguments by a trusted caller, this primitive cannot be triggered.

preconditions.necessity: If argc were checked, the NULL dereference path would be unreachable. The absence of this check is the root cause enabling the primitive.

source.description: The 8-byte unconditional load from the argv[2] string pointer reads past the string's NUL terminator when the string is shorter than 8 bytes. The read address is relative to the argv[2] string location (set by the kernel/runtime), not directly attacker-controlled.

source.root_cause: Binary has no DT_RPATH or DT_RUNPATH set (confirmed via readelf -d: 27 dynamic entries, none are RPATH/RUNPATH). NEEDED libraries libcrypto.so.1.1 and libc.so.6 are resolved via the default dynamic linker search order where LD_PRELOAD and LD_LIBRARY_PATH take precedence over system paths. An attacker who controls the execution environment can place a trojaned libcrypto.so.1.1 that executes arbitrary code at library init time (before main runs), without any memory corruption in the target binary.
source.description: Environment-layer library hijack: the dynamic linker loads attacker-controlled libcrypto.so.1.1 via LD_PRELOAD (or LD_LIBRARY_PATH in environments where cache precedence does not override it). The trojan library's __attribute__((constructor)) executes arbitrary code at load time, before main() is called. This achieves CODE_EXECUTION purely through environment control — no memory corruption, no ROP, no heap manipulation required.

Attacker-controlled trojaned libcrypto.so.1.1 loaded by linker
Trojan library __attribute__((constructor)) executes at init time before main()

controlled_element.what: The shared library loaded by the dynamic linker to satisfy the NEEDED libcrypto.so.1.1 dependency. The attacker controls the library file content (including its .init_array/.constructor code) and its placement on the linker search path (via LD_PRELOAD or LD_LIBRARY_PATH).
controlled_element.how: 1) Build a trojaned shared library with SONAME=libcrypto.so.1.1, a version script defining the OPENSSL_1_1_0 version node (required by the target's .gnu.version_r), and stub implementations of DES_set_key_unchecked/DES_ecb_encrypt to satisfy symbol resolution. 2) Add a __attribute__((constructor)) function that executes arbitrary code (e.g., system call, file write). 3) Set LD_PRELOAD=<path>/trojan_libcrypto.so.1.1 and run the target. The linker loads the trojan lib first, runs its constructor before main(), and the stub symbols override the real OpenSSL functions.

preconditions.description: Binary has no DT_RPATH or DT_RUNPATH (confirmed: readelf -d shows 27 dynamic entries, none are RPATH/RUNPATH). This is the root precondition — without it, the linker would bind to trusted absolute paths and ignore LD_LIBRARY_PATH/LD_PRELOAD for those libs.
preconditions.necessity: Without missing RPATH/RUNPATH, the linker would not consult LD_PRELOAD/LD_LIBRARY_PATH for NEEDED library resolution. This is the vulnerability itself.

preconditions.description: Attacker can control the execution environment: specifically, can set LD_PRELOAD or LD_LIBRARY_PATH, or place a file named libcrypto.so.1.1 in a directory on the linker search path.
preconditions.necessity: The hijack requires the linker to find the trojan library. LD_PRELOAD is the most reliable vector (forces load regardless of cache). LD_LIBRARY_PATH also works in environments where ld.so.cache does not override it.

preconditions.description: Trojan library must have correct SONAME (libcrypto.so.1.1) and define the OPENSSL_1_1_0 version node via a version script, because the target binary's .gnu.version_r requires version OPENSSL_1_1_0 from libcrypto.so.1.1. Without the version node, the linker finds but rejects the trojan lib.
preconditions.necessity: The target's versioned symbol requirement (OPENSSL_1_1_0) causes the linker to reject libraries that don't define this version. The trojan must satisfy this constraint.

preconditions.description: Trojan library must export the symbols the target imports (DES_set_key_unchecked, DES_ecb_encrypt) at the correct version, so the linker's symbol resolution succeeds and the program does not abort before the constructor runs.
preconditions.necessity: If symbol resolution fails, the linker aborts with an error before main. Stub implementations satisfy this — they don't need to be functionally correct, just present.

preconditions.description: No seccomp sandbox is active (confirmed: /proc/self/status shows Seccomp: 0, Seccomp_filters: 0). This allows the trojan constructor to execute arbitrary syscalls (file I/O, exec, etc.).
preconditions.necessity: If a strict seccomp filter were active, the trojan's arbitrary code might be limited to a subset of syscalls. Its absence means full code execution is possible.

preconditions.description: The binary is not setuid/setgid (confirmed: file permissions are -rwxrwxrwx, no setuid bit). The dynamic linker honors LD_PRELOAD/LD_LIBRARY_PATH for non-setuid binaries. For setuid binaries, the linker ignores these environment variables for security.
preconditions.necessity: If the binary were setuid, the linker would ignore LD_PRELOAD/LD_LIBRARY_PATH (AT_SECURE mode), and the hijack would not work via environment variables.

primitives.notes: This is an environment-layer CODE_EXECUTION primitive, not a memory-corruption primitive. It requires the attacker to control the execution environment (LD_PRELOAD or LD_LIBRARY_PATH). The root cause is the binary's missing DT_RPATH/DT_RUNPATH, which leaves NEEDED library resolution to the default linker search order. Key technical findings during verification: (1) The trojan lib must have correct SONAME (libcrypto.so.1.1) and a version script defining OPENSSL_1_1_0 — without these, the linker finds but rejects the trojan. (2) On this glibc 2.39 system, LD_LIBRARY_PATH alone did not override the cached system libcrypto (ld.so.cache took precedence after the candidate was found), but LD_PRELOAD forced unconditional load successfully. Both vectors are enabled by the same missing-RPATH root cause. (3) No seccomp, no CET, non-setuid binary — all preconditions for full code execution are met. (4) The trojan constructor runs BEFORE main(), so it executes regardless of what main does — the DES operations, write syscall, etc. are irrelevant to the primitive. (5) This primitive does not produce memory read/write/control-flow primitives in the target binary's own address space; it produces code execution in the process context via the trojan library. S4 could use this for full process compromise (the trojan can call system(), execve(), etc. directly).
